flawed_step: The claim that the stable matching is unique. Strict, complete preferences guarantee that a stable matching exists (Gale–Shapley), but they do not make it unique.
counterexample:
n=2. Men's preferences: m1: w1 > w2; m2: w2 > w1. Women's preferences: w1: m2 > m1; w2: m1 > m2.
Matching A = {(m1,w1),(m2,w2)}. The only unmatched pairs are (m1,w2) and (m2,w1). m1 prefers his partner w1 to w2, and m2 prefers his partner w2 to w1. So neither pair blocks, and A is stable.
Matching B = {(m1,w2),(m2,w1)}. The only unmatched pairs are (m1,w1) and (m2,w2). w1 prefers her partner m2 to m1, and w2 prefers her partner m1 to m2. So neither pair blocks, and B is stable.
A and B are different stable matchings, so the stable matching is not unique.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. In a 2x2 instance, each man ranks a different woman first, and each woman ranks first the man who did not rank her first. Both perfect matchings are stable: every man gets his first choice in one, and every woman gets her first choice in the other. I checked every unmatched pair in both matchings.
